props.title: Departures
props.initialSlug: Undertaker finds beauty in Japan's farewell rituals

sections.content: Departures masterfully explores death, dignity, and cultural identity through the story of a cellist who becomes a nokanshi (traditional Japanese ritual mortician). Director Yōjirō Takita crafts an emotionally resonant tale that won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film - the first Japanese film to do so. The film's power lies in how it transforms potentially morbid subject matter into a life-affirming meditation on finding meaning through serving others. Like After Life (1998) and Still Walking (2008), it uses Japanese attitudes toward death to explore deeper truths about family and purpose.

sections.content: The film's stunning cinematography by Takeshi Hamada creates a visual poetry that mirrors the grace of the ritual ceremonies. Like The Funeral (1984) by Juzo Itami, Departures uses death rituals as a lens to examine contemporary Japanese society's relationship with tradition. The protagonist's journey from reluctance to deep respect for his profession parallels films like Tampopo (1985), where mastery of a traditional craft becomes a path to self-discovery. SUBHEAD: Cultural Context and Universal Themes

While deeply rooted in Japanese culture, Departures transcends cultural boundaries much like Yi Yi (2000) and Poetry (2010), other East Asian films that find universal resonance in specific cultural experiences. The film's treatment of death recalls Mexican director Michel Franco's Chronic (2015), though Departures maintains a more optimistic outlook while dealing with similar themes of caregiving and mortality.
